summary: This 2019 Annual Review of Psychology article by Joshua Conrad Jackson, Virginia K. Choi and Michele J. Gelfand reviews social scientific research on why people take revenge, defined as motivated retaliation after a perceived harm to one's well-being. It covers biological and cultural evolutionary explanations for revenge, and the psychological and situational predictors of when people take it, including appraisals of transgressions, anger, expected pleasure, reputation and power. The authors argue for a multilevel perspective in which individual revenge acts sit within cultural systems and can change them over time. The note is truncated partway through the discussion of proximal predictors.
one_line: A 2019 Annual Review of Psychology synthesis of research on why revenge evolved and when people take it, from individual psychology to cultural systems.
key_facts: The article 'Revenge: A Multilevel Review and Synthesis' by Joshua Conrad Jackson, Virginia K. Choi and Michele J. Gelfand appeared in Annual Review of Psychology, Volume 70, 2019, pages 319-345.
The authors define revenge as motivated retaliation after a perceived harm to one's well-being, and note that self-defense and unsolicited aggression such as bullying do not count as revenge.
A 2012 study by the New York City Police Department found that 42% of the city's murders stemmed from revenge.
Across the United States, revenge is implicated in as many as 61% of school shootings and 27% of bombings.
Historical cross-cultural analyses found evidence of vengeful feuds or individual acts of vengeance in 90% of contemporary and traditional societies (Ericksen & Horton 1992).
Carlsmith et al. (2008) found that avengers begin reporting regret, rumination and negativity within a few minutes after a vengeful act, despite a short burst of positive affect.
Twin data from Eaves et al. (2008) indicate that genes account for 40% of self-reported vengefulness among men and 32% among women.
In an economic game, participants with a high-activity MAOA gene were more likely than those with a low-activity MAOA gene to dispense painful hot sauce after being provoked (McDermott et al. 2009).
Ericksen & Horton (1992) coded 186 societies in the standard cross-cultural sample and found revenge was most common in tribal groups with no institutional justice systems.
Nowak and colleagues (2016) showed in computational simulations that cultures of honor emerged fastest in simulations that included unreliable policing.
Shteynberg and colleagues (2009) found Americans were more likely to take revenge after threats to individual rights, whereas Koreans were more likely to take revenge after duty-based harms.

Brezina et al. (2004) followed 900 adolescent boys and found that boys who believed retaliatory aggression was necessary to restore honor after an insult were more likely to have injured or killed someone a year later.
Among anger, fear, sadness and frustration, anger emerged as the best emotional predictor of vengeance in Roseman et al. (1994).
Chester & DeWall (2017, p. 413) describe revenge motivated by 'the desire to return to affective homeostasis', meaning people often seek revenge to repair their negative mood.

The authors conclude that deterrence may be among the least influential of the proximal predictors of revenge, since vengeful people often feel less safe from future harm than nonvengeful people (Akin & Akin 2016).
